title: Research Bite #73: Why Peer Discussion Improves Student Performance on In-Class Concept Questions
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #73 covers M. K. Smith and colleagues' 'Why Peer Discussion Improves Student Performance on In-Class Concept Questions,' published in Science (2009, Vol. 323, pp. 122-124) -- a foundational study in the peer-instruction literature still widely cited. In an undergraduate genetics course at the University of Colorado-Boulder, 350 students answered a clicker-based concept question, discussed it with neighbors, and revoted, then individually answered a second, differently worded question testing the same underlying concept, with no answer ever revealed in between rounds. This design let the researchers rule out simple copying: if students were just parroting a confident neighbor's answer on the first question, they would have no advantage on the differently worded follow-up. Instead, performance on the fresh question rose sharply -- and strikingly, even in discussion groups where nobody initially knew the correct answer, students often converged on the right answer for the new question at rates well above chance. The conclusion is that peer discussion builds genuine conceptual understanding, not merely social influence from the most confident voice in the group.
points: The isomorphic-question design is the study's methodological masterstroke: by testing the same concept with different wording after discussion, it directly separates 'genuine understanding' from 'copying the confident student' as explanations for the improvement.

The finding that groups with nobody initially correct still converged on the right answer well above chance is the paper's most striking result -- it shows peer discussion can generate understanding that did not exist in any individual group member beforehand.

As a 2009 study still actively cited in Research Bite #73 in 2026, this paper's core finding has proven durable evidence for peer-instruction and think-pair-share style pedagogies across nearly two decades.

The result gives teachers a concrete justification for structuring peer discussion around genuinely difficult conceptual questions, not just easy ones -- the mechanism works even when no single student starts with the answer.

Because the study isolates the discussion mechanism itself (not just the clicker technology or revoting procedure), the finding generalizes to any structured peer-discussion format, not just technology-mediated ones.
quotes: When students answer a conceptual question with a clicker, discuss it with neighbours, and revote, more get it right. But is that because they have understood the idea, or because they are copying confident classmates?
In an undergraduate genetics course at the University of Colorado-Boulder, researchers tested this with 350 students.
After discussing a question, students individually answered a second, differently worded question testing the same concept, with no answers revealed in between.

Performance on this fresh question rose sharply. Crucially, even in groups where nobody initially knew the correct answer, students often reached the right answer on the new question, well above chance.
